F5.quote: The WikiWho API is currently hosted at GESIS
F5.claim: the API is hosted at GESIS (wikiwho.net) and at Wikimedia (wikiwho-api.wmcloud.org)
F5.lineage: where it runs: hosts and access

F6.quote: In the future, only Wikimedia will continue its support.
F6.claim: in future only Wikimedia will continue its support
F6.lineage: where it runs: hosts and access

F7.quote: The WikiWho API gives access to the provenance/changes of words (tokens) in Wikipedia articles.
F7.claim: what it is: an API giving the provenance and changes of words (tokens) in Wikipedia articles

F8.quote: It gives token-wise information from which revision what content originated (and thereby which editor originally authored the word) as well as all changes a token was ever subject to.
F8.claim: per token: the revision of origin, and thereby the original editor, and every change

F9.quote: An additional set of APIs delivers special HTML markup for interface applications, e.g., the browser extension WhoColor.
F9.claim: further APIs deliver HTML markup for interfaces such as WhoColor

F10.quote: Given a revisioned text document, WikiWho parses the complete set of all historical revisions (versions) in order to find out who wrote and/or removed and/or reinserted which exact text at token level at what revision.
F10.claim: the algorithm parses every historical revision to find who wrote, removed or reinserted which text, at token level, at which revision
F10.lineage: the algorithm: every revision parsed, at token level

F11.quote: along with an extensive evaluation resulting in 95% accuracy on fairly revision-rich articles.
F11.claim: its evaluation (the WWW 2014 paper): 95% accuracy on fairly revision-rich articles

F12.quote: It is implemented currently for Wikitext, but can run on any kind of text in principle (although tokenization rules might have to be adapted).
F12.claim: stated limit: implemented for wikitext; any text in principle, tokenization rules may need adapting

F13.quote: individual tokens retain a unique ID, making it possible to distinguish two tokens with identical strings in different text positions.
F13.claim: each token keeps a unique ID, so identical strings in different positions stay distinct

F14.quote: Opening a Wikipedia article it creates a color-markup on the text, showing the original authors of the content, an author list ordered by percentages of the article written and additional provenance information.
F14.claim: the WhoColor userscript colour-marks an article by original author, with an author list by percentage written

F15.quote: still poses several open research questions -- answers to which the WikiWho data can offer.
F15.claim: the identification of conflict in a changing document still poses open research questions the data can help answer

F16.quote: using "(re)delete" and "reintroduce" actions between editors to encode antagonistic and supporting actions.
F16.claim: an extension extracts relations between editors from (re)delete and reintroduce actions, antagonistic and supporting

F17.quote: WikiWho was first conceived as a dissertation project at
F17.claim: first conceived as a dissertation project at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology by Fabian Flöck and collaborators, then hosted, maintained and developed at GESIS

F18.quote: Flöck, F., & Acosta, M. (2014). WikiWho: Precise and efficient attribution of authorship of revisioned content.
F18.claim: the paper: Flöck and Acosta 2014, 'WikiWho: Precise and efficient attribution of authorship of revisioned content' (WWW 2014, pp. 843-854)
F18.lineage: the algorithm: every revision parsed, at token level

F19.quote: TokTrack: A Complete Token Provenance and Change Tracking Dataset for the English Wikipedia.
F19.claim: derived data: TokTrack, a complete token provenance and change-tracking dataset for the English Wikipedia (2017)

F20.quote: A service that provides authorship attribution of Wikipedia articles
F20.claim: what it is: a service that provides authorship attribution of Wikipedia articles

F21.quote: WikiWho is a service providing authorship attribution using a content persistence algorithm.
F21.claim: what it is: a service providing authorship attribution by a content persistence algorithm

F22.quote: It was first developed by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and GESIS – Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences
F22.claim: first developed by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and GESIS

F23.quote: In August 2021, it was moved to Wikimedia Cloud Services infrastructure and is now maintained and under further development by Community Tech and the Wiki Education Foundation
F23.claim: moved to Wikimedia Cloud Services in August 2021; maintained and developed by Community Tech and the Wiki Education Foundation

F24.claim: the infobox's group: Moderator Tools and the Wiki Education Foundation

F25.quote: find out who wrote and/or removed and/or reinserted which exact text at token level at what revision
F25.claim: the core: parsing all historical revisions of a wiki page to find who wrote, removed or reinserted which text at token level
F25.lineage: the algorithm: every revision parsed, at token level

F26.quote: This means that for every token (such as a word), its individual addition, removal, and reintroduction history becomes available.
F26.claim: for every token its addition, removal and reintroduction history becomes available

F27.quote: The original algorithm working behind the scenes is described in a WWW 2014 paper , along with an extensive evaluation resulting in 95% accuracy on fairly revision-rich articles.
F27.claim: the algorithm is described in a WWW 2014 paper with an evaluation of 95% accuracy on fairly revision-rich articles

F28.quote: The WikiWho APIs and OpenAPI documentation may be found at https://wikiwho.wmcloud.org/
F28.claim: the APIs and their documentation are at wikiwho.wmcloud.org
F28.lineage: where it runs: hosts and access

F29.quote: Instead of annotated, tokenized wikitext, the WhoColor API delivers annotated HTML of a wiki article that can be read by a browser.
F29.claim: WhoColor, a service on top of the core data, delivers annotated HTML of an article for a browser

F30.quote: The WhoColor API is what powers the Who Wrote That? tool as well as features within the Wiki Education Dashboard and Programs and Events Dashboard
F30.claim: the WhoColor API powers the Who Wrote That? tool and features of the Wiki Education and Programs and Events Dashboards

F31.claim: supported wikis: a list of 71 entries, 70 distinct (Swedish Wikipedia listed twice), Afrikaans to Welsh, English among them

F32.claim: tools powered by WikiWho: Who Wrote That?, XTools Authorship, XTools Blame, Programs & Events Dashboard, Wiki Education Dashboard, the pywikibot.Page.authorship() method

F34.quote: This research aims to provide an API for retrieving provenance and change information of single tokens in any arbitrary Wikipedia article revision.
F34.claim: what it is: research to provide an API for provenance and change information of single tokens in any Wikipedia article revision

F35.quote: This page documents a research project in progress

F38.quote: this can also be used for extracting disputes about content.

F39.quote: We currently offer the service in English, German, Turkish and Basque, with more languages planned.
